title: Fine-grained dual-phase steels fabricated via cold-rolling ferrite-martensite structure and subsequent intercritical annealing
abstract: A proposed alternative method for processing dual phase (DP) steels is the utilization of a cold-rolled duplex ferrite-martensite structure, followed by intercritical annealing. The obtained results demonstrate the feasibility of this approach in producing a desirable microstructure. The microstructure consists of ferrite grains with an average size of less than 6 μm, along with a uniformly distributed fine martensitic phase. Treatment of the steels using this alternative route results in improved strength-ductility properties and a greater work-hardening exponent. These steels exhibit an excellent combination of mechanical properties with tensile strength of 866.69 MPa, total elongation of 24.40%, and the product of tensile strength and total elongation of exceed 20 GPa%.
journal: Journal of Materials Research and Technology

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Dual phase (DP) steels are characterized by their unique microstructure, which consists of both hard martensite and soft ferrite phases [ 1 , 2 ]. This composite microstructure gives DP steels distinct mechanical properties that make them advantageous compared to conventional high strength low alloy steels. These include characteristics such as continuous yielding, low yield stress to tensile strength ratios, and high ductility [ 3–5 ]. To meet the specific design requirements of different components, various grades of DP steels with different tensile strengths and formability are produced industrially. These differences in mechanical properties are primarily achieved by controlling the carbon content [ 6 , 7 ], alloying elements [ 8–10 ], or adjusting the martensite fraction [ 11–13 ] within the steel. Typically, increasing the martensite fraction leads to higher strength in the steel, but it often comes at the cost of reduced ductility.

To further enhance the mechanical properties of DP steel, several different approaches have been explored, with the main focus being on refining the microstructure. Shin et al. [ 14 ] and Park et al. [ 15 ] have utilized techniques such as Equal Channel Angular Pressing (ECAP) or Accumulative Roll Bonding (ARB) [ 16 ], combined with intercritical annealing, to develop fine-grained DP steel. Mazaheri [ 17 ] and Lan et al. [ 18 ] have employed cold deformation of martensite as an initial microstructure to fabricate ultrafine-grained DP steels. In addition, the deformation induced ferrite transformation (DIFT) technique [ 19 ] and large strain warm deformation technique [ 20 ] have also been utilized to create fine-grained DP steels. Meng [ 21 ] and Azizi-Alizamani et al. [ 22 ] have reported a method that involves rapid annealing to enhance the mechanical properties of DP steel. These various approaches aim to improve the strength and ductility of DP steel by refining the microstructure through specific processing techniques.

Indeed, while the techniques mentioned above have been shown to be effective in refining the grain size and improving the tensile properties of DP steel, they can present challenges when it comes to industrial production. Many of these techniques require complex processes and specialized equipment, which may not be readily available or feasible on a large scale. One specific challenge that arises in the cold deformation of martensite is the occurrence of edge cracks and the need for larger rolling forces. These factors can limit the practicality and cost-effectiveness of this particular approach.

Fine-grained DP steels are difficult to produce because of complex and sophisticated control process. However, in the present study, we describe a simple process and elucidate the relationship between microstructure and mechanical properties.

sections.heading: Experimental
paragraphs:
The experimental material used in this study was a hot rolled strip steel with an initial thickness of 4.0 mm. The microstructure of the material consisted of a combination of ferrite and pearlite. The chemical composition of the steel used in the experiment is provided in  Table 1 
                      .

AC 1  and AC 3  temperatures were determined by a Formastor-FII dilatometer and is presented in  Fig. 1 
                      .

In this work, the annealing process used for producing different steel samples, including the conventional annealed steel (DPI), DPII steel, and DPIII steel, is illustrated in  Fig. 2 
                      .

The DPI steel sample was obtained through a conventional annealing process. Initially, the hot rolled strip with a ferrite-pearlite microstructure and a thickness of 4.0 mm was cold rolled to a thickness of 1.2 mm, resulting in a reduction of 70%. This cold-rolled sample was then annealed at a temperature of 770 °C for a duration of 5 min. After annealing, the sample was immediately water-quenched.

For the new annealing process, the as-received hot rolled strip steel was subjected to an intercritical annealing treatment. The hot rolled strip was heated to a temperature of 770 °C and held at this temperature for 10 min. Subsequently, the sample was water quenched. The purpose of this intercritical annealing was to induce duplex microstructures. Next, the sample was cold-rolled to reduce its thickness and was further annealed to obtained the desired microstructure.

Microstructures were characterized using a Leica DM 2500 M metallographic microscope (OM) and a FEI Quanta 600 scanning electron microscope (SEM). The samples were prepared via ground and polished, and then etched using the LePera’s reagent (1% aqueous solution of sodium metabisulfite and 4% picric acid in ethyl alcohol) and 4% Nital solution. The microstructure characterization was also observed by a FEI Tecnai G2F20S–TWIN transmission electron microscopy (TEM).

Tensile specimens according to GB T228-2002 standard were cut from the annealed plates with a nominal gauge length of 25 mm and nominal width of 5 mm. The tensile test was carried out at a cross head speed of 2 mm min −1  using a 100 kN Instron tensile machine. All specimens were tested to failure. During the tensile experiments, force and displacement plots were recorded, from which stress and strain data was obtained.

sections.heading: Microstructure
paragraphs:
Fig. 3 
                          shows the ferrite-pearlite and ferrite-martensite microstructures after cold rolling, the aspect ratio of the ferrite grains is consistent with the macroscopic level of cold reduction, further, the pearlite or martensite are also elongated, suggesting that ferrite and pearlite/martensite co-deform.  Fig. 3 (c) and (d) present the TEM images of the deformed martensite, where the martensite laths underwent a more severe and uniform deformation, shear-banding and severe sliding have taken place, even dense dislocation cell structures with mean diameter of around 500 nm are distinguished. These microstructures might provide abundant nucleation sites for the ferrite and austenite to nucleate during annealing and led to a finer grain.

In  Fig. 3 , the microstructures of the steel samples after cold rolling are shown. The ferrite-pearlite and ferrite-martensite structures are observed, and the aspect ratio of the ferrite grains is found to be consistent with the degree of cold reduction at the macroscopic level. This indicates that the ferrite grains deform in a similar manner to the reduction in thickness during cold rolling. Similarly, the pearlite (in the ferrite-pearlite structure) or martensite (in the ferrite-martensite structure) is also elongated, suggesting that co-deformation of ferrite and pearlite/martensite occurs during the cold rolling process.

TEM images, specifically  Fig. 3 (c) and (d), provide further insight into the deformation of the martensite. The martensite laths are observed to undergo a more severe and uniform deformation. This deformation is characterized by shear-banding and significant sliding, indicating plastic deformation processes occurring within the martensite structure. Additionally, the TEM images show the presence of dense dislocation cell structures with a mean diameter of approximately 500 nm. These dislocation cell structures are a result of the severe deformation imposed on the martensite during cold rolling. The deformed microstructures provide numerous sites for the nucleation of ferrite and austenite during annealing. As a result, during the annealing process, the formation of finer grain sizes in the microstructure is facilitated.

Fig. 4 
                          shows the microstructure of the steel after annealing. Compared DPI steel, DPII and DPIII steels have a ﬁne grain structure and martensite uniformly dispersed in the ﬁnal microstructure. According to a quantitative measurement by image-pro-plus, the amount of martensite in DPII and DPIII samples were increased from 23% to 27% and 30%, while the ferrite grain sizes were obviously reﬁned to 7.8 μm and 5.4 μm from 19.8 μm as compared with the conventional annealing process with ferrite-pearlite initial microstructure.

sections.heading: Tensile properties
paragraphs:
The tensile stress-strain curve of all the steels are depicted in  Fig. 5 
                         . It is clear that all grades exhibit a continuous yielding behavior and no yield point elongation is observed. The strength of DPII and DPIII steels is much higher than that of DPI steel, although there is a slight drop in the elongation. The yield strength YS of DPIII steel increases from 340.69 MPa to 418.22 MPa (22.8% higher), and the ultimate tensile strength TS improves from 628.63 MPa to 866.69 MPa with 238.06 MPa higher (37.9%). The total elongation of all the steels lies on the same level (24%–26%). In summary, DPIII steel obtained best combination of mechanical properties, whose product of tensile strength and total elongation was 21.15 GPa%, a signiﬁcant improvement compared to DPI steel.

It is known that the strength of ferrite–martensite dual phase steel in mainly depends on the volume fraction of martensite. However, the ductility of the DP steel is combined results of many factors. Among them are the dispersion of martensite, the grain size of ferrite and martensite particles. A high volume fraction of martensite and better distribution of fine martensite particles which led to a better tensile performance of DPII and DPIII steel as compared to DPI steel.

As shown in  Fig. 6 
                         , the data of TS and TS × TE vs. TE are plotted to compare the DP steels developed in this study with the previous works or commercial steels, DP600, DP800 [ 15 , 20 , 23–25 ]. All steels have the comparable chemical contents. It is obvious that the results of the DP structures in this study are comparable to those reported in the literature. Another important aspect is the distribution of the respective phases (martensite and ferrite). A homogeneous distribution of the phases is necessary to achieve promising mechanical properties. The strength–elongation balance is higher in the present study as compared to others, i.e. when a truly homogeneous fine DP structure is predominantly attained.

The aforementioned mechanical properties of the newly developed DP steels, together with the commercially used DP600 and DP800 steels, which have the same volume fraction of martensite, clearly indicate the good potential of the new DP steels for application in automobile body structure.

sections.heading: Summary
paragraphs: The current study aimed to investigate the feasibility of intercritical annealing following cold deformation of ferrite-martensite duplex in order to enhance the mechanical properties of DP590 steels. The proposed route resulted in a significant improvement in the microstructure.

The samples treated by the proposed route exhibited a much finer ferrite grain size and fine, uniformly distributed martensite islands compared to the conventional annealing process with a ferrite-pearlite initial microstructure. The amount of martensite in the samples increased from 23% to 30%, while the ferrite grain sizes were notably refined to 5.4 μm from 19.8 μm.

As a result of these microstructural improvements, the processed low-carbon steel demonstrated a better strength-ductility trade-off and a greater work-hardening exponent. In fact, steel treated at 800 °C was characterized by best combination of mechanical properties with tensile strength of 866.69 MPa, total elongation of 24.40%, and the product of tensile strength and total elongation exceed approximately 20 GPa%.

Overall, the findings of this study indicate that the proposed intercritical annealing route, following cold deformation of the ferrite-martensite duplex, is an effective method for enhancing the mechanical properties of DP590 steels. The refined microstructure and improved strength-ductility trade-off make this processed low-carbon steel a promising material for the requirement of the automotive industry.
